page: Google Cloud Platform n4-standard-32 is a general-purpose server instance belonging to the n4 family. It features 32 dedicated x86_64 vCPUs powered by an Intel processor, structured as 16 physical cores with 2 threads per core. The instance is equipped with 128 GB of RAM, providing a balanced memory-to-core ratio of 4.0 GB per vCPU. It does not include local storage or bundled GPUs, and offers zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses. The processor features a 260 MB L3 cache, 2 MB L2 cache, and 48 KB L1d cache, alongside hardware-accelerated instruction sets including Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions and Advanced Vector Extensions.

Benchmark data indicates strong performance in memory bandwidth for large blocks, with uncached read-only speeds reaching 211.52 GB/sec and write speeds at 99.63 GB/sec, both placing in the top 25 percent. Static web serving throughput is also strong at 44.06 GB/sec, alongside strong image processing scores in Geekbench. Most other compute metrics, including single-core and multi-core stress-ng tests, software compilation, and database operations, fall within the average middle 50 percent range.

While the instance demonstrates strong capabilities in small-model LLM text generation at 296.22 tokens per second, it exhibits a significant performance tradeoff when handling large-scale models. Specifically, LLM inference text generation for a 70B model drops to a poor 2.31 tokens per second, placing it in the bottom 10 percent of benchmarked systems. This profile makes the n4-standard-32 suitable for general-purpose workloads, web serving, and moderate database operations, but less effective for large-scale LLM text generation without dedicated GPU acceleration.

The processor includes a 260 MB L3 cache and supports Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions and AVX-512. In benchmarks, the instance demonstrates strong performance in large-block memory bandwidth, static web serving throughput, and small-model LLM text generation. However, most general compute, database, and compilation benchmarks fall within the average range. A notable tradeoff is its poor performance in large-model LLM text generation, which drops to the bottom 10 percent at 2.31 tokens per second. This instance is suited for general-purpose workloads, web serving, and moderate database operations.
